title: “Bells”: Prelude and Fugue No.2, Book II
content_blocks: Writing this pair of pieces probably provided the most fun of any piece I’ve ever written. While experimenting with my piano preparations, I discovered that sticking chopsticks in between the strings could produce magically-beautiful bell-like sounds—and that different chopsticks and/or different positions in the strings would produce different bell sounds. Research for these pieces therefore required going to many different Chinese, Japanese, and Korean restaurants—what can I say? we all suffer for our art!
As I was beginning the composition, I came across the poem “Night-Mooring at Maple Bridge” by the Tang Dynasty poet Zhang Ji (766–830; translation is my own):
The moon sets, a crow caws, and the dark sky is filled with frost;
On maple trees shines light from an angler, in sad sleep lost.
From the temple on far Cold Mountain, outside of Suzhou,
Midnight bell sounds reach my trav’ler’s boat, on the river tossed.

Since the chopsticks—and golf tees and straws—obscure the notes actually played, for the prelude I thought that I would paradoxically create a highly-structured composition.  I find the result fascinating:  we get glimpses of the structure of the notes played by the pianist, but they seem transformed and shrouded by the preparations, just as any pattern in the bell sounds from the temple on far Cold Mountain are veiled by the distance and geography.

Although the fugue is also quite carefully structured, the subject is explicitly inspired by the poem.  It begins with a three-fold repetition of a single note, each delayed more and more from the previous note, evoking a bell on a buoy in a river clanging from the motion of a wave, and then slowing down and fading away.

The lowest bell sound heard—on a low D, the nominal key of the piece—is not heard until the final few measures of the piece.  While the musical/poetic reason for this should be clear (the lowest note adding a tone of finality to the pair of pieces), there is an important practical reason:  the lower strings require larger chopsticks in order for the timbral changes to work, but the 12-to-14 inch cooking chopsticks used on the low D have so high a center of gravity that it is hard to get them to stay in place after playing the note more than a few times.

Mika Sasaki’s beautiful performances of the Prelude and Fugue can be seen on YouTube. Rob Baker of UCLA has made a video with me demonstrating some of the preparations used for this piece and others, and performing just the fugue, twice: one with the chopstick preparations and one without. They don’t compare with Mika’s performances, but they serve well to demonstrate just how different the prepared and unprepared pianos can be.
The chopsticks obscure the notes actually played.  We get glimpses of the structure of the notes played by the pianist, but they seem transformed and shrouded by the preparations.
